prompt: Savitch’s reachability algorithm halves its path-length bound at each level and stores only a few vertex names and counters per frame. Why does it use squared-logarithmic working space?

options.text: It stores the whole search tree in compressed form
options.explanation: It stores only the currently active recursion stack.

options.text: There are logarithmically many frames, each needing logarithmically many bits
options.explanation: The depth and per-frame costs multiply; sequential branches reuse storage.

options.text: It has one visited bit per graph vertex
options.explanation: That is not the midpoint-recursion workspace strategy.

options.text: It always finishes in logarithmic time
options.explanation: Saving memory can require extensive repeated computation.

workedExample: At each level the permitted path length halves, giving logarithmic stack depth. Each frame remembers only a few vertex names and the current length, requiring logarithmic bits. The product gives squared-logarithmic space. This is abstract workspace; Python frames are larger, and the repeated midpoint search may take much longer than a visited-set traversal.

prompt: Savitch’s theorem replaces a nondeterministic space bound by its square. What does this imply for a problem using polynomial nondeterministic space?

options.text: The deterministic algorithm must use exactly the same space
options.explanation: Savitch guarantees a quadratic increase in the bound, not equality at the same degree.

options.text: It has a deterministic polynomial-space algorithm
options.explanation: Squaring a fixed polynomial still gives a polynomial; this proves PSPACE equals NPSPACE.

options.text: It has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm
options.explanation: The simulation may recompute extensively; the theorem bounds memory.
The guaranteed space increase is quadratic, not exponential.

workedExample: Savitch stores a recursion stack whose depth is proportional to the original space bound, with a few configurations of that size per frame. Squaring a polynomial still gives a polynomial. Thus nondeterministic polynomial space can be simulated in deterministic polynomial space, without proving the same degree or polynomial time.
